brief: BofA's Hartnett frames "bonds end bubbles": rising yields are breaking the market's speculative edges (Korean bonds, French OAT-Bund spreads, CCC credit) while the core holds, because hikes haven't yet dented US hard data, forward EPS, or hyperscaler capex estimates. BofA's rates team says the rise is mostly growth-driven, and that Jackson Hole "cut the anchor line" (Powell's old restrictive guidance vs Warsh's doubt), so yields keep rising until data or markets say stop. That is BofA's "hike or bond spike" dilemma: if data stays strong the Fed must hike or risk a bond spike, even though markets price only 17% for an Oct 28 hike versus 81% for Dec 9. Hartnett ranks an October hike to cap yields as the most bullish event into year-end. Separately, BofA says France's 140bps OAT-Bund spread reflects two decades of fiscal time inconsistency, expects it to settle 100-150bps with ECB backstops if it overshoots, yet still upgraded French stocks, arguing the Stoxx 600 drop reflects US yields, not French risk. EPFR shows the largest dash to cash since April 2020. Hartnett calls the Nov 3 midterms, where markets price a 64% Democratic sweep, the likely 10%+ catalyst, and argues that outcome would be the most bearish, not the market's own read.
